title: The Bodega–Ross Corridor
subtitle: The port Spain discovered and never held, 1775–1841
abstract: Companion map to a research article on the 1793 Bodega expedition. It follows one stretch of coast for sixty-six years: Bodega y Quadra charts the port in 1775; Spain attempts and abandons an occupation in 1793; Russian hunters and then Colony Ross (1812) move into the vacuum; Spanish probes reconnoiter but never dislodge them; the Russians finally leave by sale in 1841. Coast Miwok communities appear throughout as intelligence sources, guides, and negotiators on their own account. Features are drawn from the same verified datasets as the other maps and keep their citations.

features.name: Goycoechea's Overland Expedition to Bodega
features.summary: 10 soldiers + sergeant march overland from SF via Bolinas and Tomales Bay to Bodega. Coast Miwok direct them to harder western route; later admitted "deceived." Territory 45 miles north of SF is "tierra incognita."
features.result: "Tierra incognita"; Spain's own governor admits unknown territory

features.name: Eliza's Activo at Bodega · Spain's Last Pacific Exploration
features.summary: Eliza arrives in Activo after near-starvation NW Coast voyage. Spain's last Pacific exploration. The exhausted vessel barely makes it to Bodega; the empire's reach is collapsing.
features.result: Last Spanish Pacific exploration; barely survived

sources.citation: Wagner 1931; C-A 14.

features.name: Golden Gate Crossing · Borrowed Launches
features.summary: 32 horses ferried across the Golden Gate using launches borrowed from visiting San Blas frigates Princesa and Aranzazu. Spain cannot cross its own bay without foreign ships.
features.result: Spain depends on visiting vessels to cross its own frontier

sources.citation: C-A 14 p. 113. Arrillaga.

features.name: Viceroy Orders Bodega · "Whether or Not English Are There"
features.summary: Revilla Gigedo orders Bodega occupied. Full fortification plan for Bodega + SF + Monterey + SD. Never executed. Supplies eventually repurposed (June 10, 1794).
features.result: Order given; never carried out

sources.citation: C-A 22, ii.144–148; bodega-failure-1793.

features.name: English at Bodega "con los cañones en tierra"
features.summary: Arrillaga reports an English vessel anchored at Bodega with "cannons on land." Identity uncertain; Colnett traces? New vessel? Rumor? Same year as Spanish Bodega failure.
features.result: Foreign military presence in territory Spain cannot reach

features.name: Zúñiga Shows Bodega Plans to British · No Concealment
features.summary: San Diego commandant Zúñiga freely shows Bodega harbor plans to British officers. No concealment at all; contradicts the tight security at SF. The policy was inconsistent.
features.result: Concealment policy fails at San Diego

sources.citation: Menzies 1924:335.

features.name: RAC Fur-Collecting Begins at Bodega
features.summary: 130 Aleut hunters aboard Kodiak. First Russian representative: Tarakanov. 40+ Russians + 150 Indians by 1809 (Argüello report). Moraga protests; ignored.
features.result: Permanent Russian presence established; Spain protests but cannot act

sources.citation: Milliken 2009:22–25; C-A 12.

features.name: 130 Bidarkas in San Francisco Bay
features.summary: 130 Aleut bidarkas (kayaks) hunting sea otter inside San Francisco Bay. The Russians are inside Spain's premier port and Spain cannot stop them.
features.result: Russian hunting inside the Bay; sovereignty violated

sources.citation: C-A 12 (Prov. St. Pap. XIX).

features.name: Farallon Islands · Russian Sealing Station
features.summary: Russian sealing station on the Farallones; 18 miles off the coast of San Francisco. Aleut hunters camped seasonally. Spain/Mexico never contested it.
features.result: Russian territory visible from SF; unchallenged

sources.citation: Bancroft II; Fort Ross sources.

features.name: Hagemeister Treaty with Kashaya Pomo
features.summary: Hagemeister convened the chiefs at Ross and had a protocol drawn recording their consent to the Company's occupation, with Spanish authority nowhere in the instrument. The protocol was signed by the Russian witnesses and the chiefs assented orally, so it is better described as recorded consent than as a mutually signed treaty. Medals reading allies of Russia were given out in 1819. Russia grounded its title here in recorded indigenous consent, where Spain grounded its own in the bull of 1493.
features.result: Russia treats Pomo as sovereign; Spain does not exist here

sources.citation: Protocol of the meeting at Colony Ross between the Indian tribal chiefs and Captain-Lieutenant Hagemeister, 22 September 1817; Archive of Foreign Policy of the Russian Empire (AVPRI), reprinted in the Fort Ross Conservancy's 2012 bicentennial collection of documents, and in Istomin, Gibson and Tishkov (eds.), Russian California 1806-1860: A History in Documents (Moscow, 2005).
Glenn Farris, 'The Russian Imprint on the Colonization of California', and his discussion of the 1817 protocol and the 1819 medals.

features.name: Kuskov's RAC Letters to the SF Commandant
features.summary: Ivan Kuskov, the Russian-American Company's man at Ross, corresponds directly with the San Francisco commandant. He had received the French-language letter sent through Moraga and Gervasio Argüello but had no interpreter for it; he sends the Company's confidential agent Slobodchikov to San Francisco with a boat and three bidarkas to settle the balance due, offering goods by the enclosed invoice or two oxen instead; and he presses again for the return of the Kodiak men, adding that if Arrillaga has truly ordered it they should be forwarded, and if not, 'it is my duty to inform my superior officers and the Home Government'. Ross writing to a Spanish presidio as one administration to another.
features.result: Ross corresponds with San Francisco as one administration with another

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 1218-20 / Savage pp. 369-370 / scan n376-n377, Doc 440. Iván Kuskov, 8 June 1814, in the English translation by Iván Pisteff that Savage copied.

features.name: Spanish Missions Supply Kuskov at Fort Ross
features.summary: The Spanish missions supplying Kuskov's Russian colony; Spain's own establishments provisioning the foreign outpost on the ground it claimed. The open coast as routine economic fact, running in Spain's disfavor.
features.result: Spain provisions the colony it was ordered to uproot

features.name: Fort Ross Abandonment Resolved
features.summary: The RAC Main Board resolves to abandon Ross and "sell or barter for wheat to the inhabitants of San Francisco." The otter gone, Ross is liquidated; the economic close of the arc that opened with the resource.
features.result: Russia leaves; Ross sold to Sutter, a promoter of the US invasion

sources.citation: Fort Ross AVPRI, 1841 abandonment resolution (via Gibson & Istomin).

features.name: RAC Parlamentario · Podushkin on the Chirikoff at Monterey
features.summary: Baranov, from Novo-Arkhangelsk, protests the "insults to the Russian Flag and the capture and keeping in cruel bondage of Russians… in the waters and the coasts of California," invokes the 1812 treaty, and sends Lt. Podushkin as a parlamentario aboard the Chirikoff to Monterey. Russia negotiating as a commercial sovereign on Spain's claimed coast.
features.result: Russia treats with Spain as an equal power on the California coast

sources.citation: C-A 13 Docs 263–264 (Podushkin's request, 22 Apr 1817; Baranov's protest, 2 Feb 1817).

features.name: Yanovsky's RAC Trade Overture
features.summary: RAC chief manager Semyon Yanovsky proposes a joint, equal-shares otter-hunt and open commerce (via Khlebnikov and the Madrid embassy; the Ilmena to supply Ross). Solá replies he cannot grant otter-hunting; only the Viceroy can. The third volume of one continuous Russo-Spanish negotiation.
features.result: Russia again negotiates as a commercial sovereign; Spain defers to Mexico City

sources.citation: C-A 55 Docs 333–334 (Yanovsky / Solá, ~1820).

features.name: The Suvorov at SF + the RAC Proclamation to California
features.summary: The Russian ship Suvorov, from St Petersburg under Lazarev, anchored at San Francisco on 20 August 1815 asking water, wood and provisions, which were promised. She carried a formal passport and proclamation from the Company's directors, addressed «á nuestros buenos amigos y vecinos, los nobles y honrados Españoles habitantes de Cal.», to our good friends and neighbours, the noble and honoured Spaniards inhabiting California. The address invokes the long Russo-Spanish friendship, the treaty of Veliky Luki of 1812, the Battle of Vitoria with Jourdan's baton and 130 cannon taken, Napoleon's catastrophe in Russia, the regiment of Spanish prisoners named for Alexander, and Wellington crossing the Pyrenees; then it recounts Rezanov's visit to San Francisco in 1806 and the bid to open commerce between California and the Company's colonies at Kodiak and Sitka. The institutional Russian demand for the California provision trade, arriving by ship.
features.result: The Company's formal trade overture delivered at San Francisco

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. p. 1404 / Savage pp. 395-396 / scan n402-n403, Doc 486. Luis Argüello on the arrival of the Russian ship, 21 August 1815.

Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 1405-10 / Savage pp. 396-399 / scan n403-n408, Doc 487. The passport and proclamation of the Suvorov, signed by the Company's directors Buldakov, Kramer and Zelensky under Alexander I, St Petersburg, 12 July 1811; the English above is a translation of the Spanish Savage copied.

features.name: Rezanov Arrives on Juno
features.summary: Nikolai Rezanov; Imperial Chamberlain, RAC shareholder, diplomat. Arrives at SF. Concepción Argüello courtship. Intelligence gathering on Spanish defenses. First Russian official at SF.
features.result: Russia assesses Spanish California firsthand

sources.citation: Bancroft II; Gibson & Istomin 2014.

features.name: Coast Miwok Intelligence to Sal
features.summary: An Indian 'de las Islas' came before the presidio and told Sal there were two ships at Bodega. Sal's own report: the man answered that they did not understand what was said to them, «y q.e los soldados traían ropa como nuestras vueltas, de q.e colegí serían ingleses», that the soldiers wore clothing like our facings, from which Sal inferred they must be English. Asked again, the informant said the ships had been there four moons and were no longer there, that they had taken water and wood and killed many deer, and that they had asked the Indians for cattle, showing them cattle horns. The English identification is Sal's inference from the clothing, not something the informant said, and «vueltas» is most likely the turned-back facings of a uniform; it is not a report of clothes worn inside out. Indigenous intelligence reaching the presidio three weeks ahead of the official channel.
features.result: Native networks ahead of imperial intelligence; the nationality a Spanish inference

sources.citation: St. Pap., Sac. (BANC MSS C-A 55), tomo vi, orig. pp. 67-68 / scan n66-n67, Doc 124. Hermenegildo Sal, San Francisco, 8 October 1792, «Buques ingleses en Bodega». Savage prints Sal's first-person report inside quotation marks; leaf re-read at full resolution.

features.name: Coast Miwok Deceive Goycoechea
features.summary: The Coast Miwok told Goycoechea, through his interpreter, that there was a vessel at the mouth of the port and that if he went their way he could speak to its captain, 'as the lagoon joined the sea and we could not cross it'. He went that way, down the west side of Tomales Bay, against instructions that had ordered him up the east side, and found he could not get round. Meeting Matute on 8 August he consulted him 'about the deceit practiced on me by the natives who had assured me that I could not cross the lagoon because it made a turn and entered the sea'. Wagner, editing him, suggests he may simply have misunderstood them. Either way, the route the Spanish party took that week was settled by what the people of the lagoon told it.
features.result: A Spanish march routed by local information, mistaken or given

sources.citation: Goycoechea's diary, 6 to 8 August 1793, AGN Sección Historia vol. 70, translated in Wagner, CHSQ 10, no. 4 (1931), 342-44, with the editor's notes 69 and 73.

features.name: Coast Miwok Calibrated Diplomacy at Bodega
features.summary: Coast Miwok "prepared to give us battle"; choose instead to present pinole and fruit. Not submission; calibrated response. They evaluated the Spanish party and chose diplomacy.
features.result: Military capability held in reserve; diplomacy chosen

features.name: Coast Miwok Bilingual Intermediaries at Tomales
features.summary: Coast Miwok calling "Amico," speaking Spanish, pointing up lagoon repeating "Spaniard." Bilingual intermediaries positioning between British and Spanish empires. They know both powers and broker between them.
features.result: Trilingual positioning between empires

sources.citation: Menzies 1924:302.

features.name: Guirmenes Intel on Bodega · "Keep This Indian Happy"
features.summary: Indigenous informant (Guirmenes) reports no foreign ship at Bodega for 2 years. Governor orders: "previene se tenga á ese indio contento" (keep this Indian happy). Indigenous surveillance network sustained across years; Spain depends on it.
features.result: Spain pays for indigenous intelligence

features.name: Chief Vallí-éla Requests Russian Flag
features.summary: Chief Vallí-éla of Bodega Miwok requests Russian protection and asks Golovnin for a Russian flag. "Very glad to have Russian neighbors." Three independent accounts (Golovnin, Matiushkin, Lütke). The indigenous chief chooses his empire.
features.result: Indigenous imperial choice; requests Russian protection

sources.citation: Golovnin 1979:165 via Farris 1998:6; Archive of Foreign Policy of the Russian Empire (AVPRI), the Golovnin materials.

features.name: Menzies Lands at Bodega
features.summary: Menzies landed from the Chatham with Lieutenant Puget on 20 October 1793, in a bay whose latitude they fixed by observation at 38 deg. 19' 30" N. On the bluff headland they found a cross lately put up, made of a piece of a cask stave lashed to a pole with a rope yarn, and the brush burned off around it; Wagner, reading Goycoechea and Matute alongside, puts that cross on Bodega Head. Walking down to the channel they met a party of Coast Miwok who sat down at their approach and called out 'Amico', friend, a word Menzies had no doubt they had from the Spaniards, and who pointed repeatedly up the lagoon when they spoke of Spaniards. Four miles further south the Chatham passed the mouth of the next opening, about a mile wide, without entering it. The 1924 editor's footnote glossing the inland water as Tomales Bay is why this landing is often placed there.
features.result: British find evidence of failed Spanish expedition

sources.citation: Menzies' California journal, California Historical Society Quarterly 2, no. 4 (1924), 301-04.
Wagner, 'The Last Spanish Exploration of the Northwest Coast', CHSQ 10, no. 4 (1931), 338: Menzies at Bodega Bay on 20 October 1793, and the cross on Bodega Head.

features.name: HMS Raccoon at San Francisco
features.summary: British warship from Columbia River. HMS Raccoon had seized Fort Astoria Dec 1813. Needed gunpowder. Crew deserting to Spanish protection as "Roman Catholics." Written in English in the archive.
features.result: British warship uses SF as supply port; War of 1812 reaches Pacific

sources.citation: C-A 12; ca12-russian-california-documents.

features.name: Kotzebue Visits on Rurik
features.summary: Otto von Kotzebue arrives at SF on scientific circumnavigation. Spain demands Ross abandonment. Diplomatic failure; Russia ignores the demand.
features.result: Spanish diplomatic protest; Russia ignores it

sources.citation: James R. Gibson and Alexei A. Istomin (eds.), Russian California, 1806-1860: A History in Documents (Hakluyt Society), Doc. 32.

features.name: Colnett's Argonaut at Bodega
features.summary: British ship takes refuge during storm; cuts spars, makes repairs. Later misidentified by Spanish as active English threat. Ghost presence that haunted Spanish intelligence for years.

features.name: Solá to the Viceroy: San Rafael and the Russians in One Despatch
features.summary: One despatch carries both the new establishment at San Rafael and the warning about the Russian posts at Ross and Bodega. That the two concerns travelled together is the fact; that the mission was founded for the Russians is a further claim the letter does not settle. Bancroft, reading the same report, gives the health of the San Francisco neophytes as doubtless the true reason for the foundation and attributes the anti-Russian motive to Russian writers rather than to the Spanish record.
features.result: Two concerns in one despatch; the motive contested, not proved

sources.citation: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 25), tomo ix, orig. pp. 583-604 / scan n429-n449, Doc 756: Solá's report to the Viceroy, Monterey, 3 April 1818, on the Russian establishments at Ross and Bodega.
Bancroft, History of California II (1885), 328-30, for the health reason and the Russian-writers attribution.

features.name: Colony Ross (Russian benchmark)
features.summary: The measuring stick. A single Russian-American Company outpost, founded September 1812. Gabriel Moraga's eyewitness reconnaissance of 30 July 1814 describes a firm wooden quadrangle with two corner torreones of four cannon each and about twenty-six embrasures, the other two corners empty; an interior galpón serving as barracks and warehouse; vegetable gardens; bidarkas of sea-lion hide; about forty personas de razón and many Kodiaks; some thirty cattle and horses in a separate enclosure; a night sentinel at Kuskov's house; and the ship gone to Sitka with grain and furs. His military judgement was about the approach rather than the walls: artillery could not be brought up without a better road. A 1813 Spanish intelligence report had credited the post with about thirteen mounted cannon. Either figure matches or exceeds the serviceable artillery of the whole San Francisco defence in the same decade.
series: ~95 Russians + ~80 Aleut hunters; stockade ~150 yards square
~13 mounted cannon (Spanish intelligence estimate, Viceroy Calleja)
8 cannon in two corner towers + ~26 embrasures; 'not easy to attack' (Moraga, eyewitness)
features.result: One Russian post the equal of the principal Spanish fort, in guns and in men

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 1215-17 / Savage pp. 364, 367-368 / scan n371, Doc 439. Gabriel Moraga's reconnaissance and defence assessment of the Russian post at Ross, San Francisco, 30 July 1814 (unsigned).
Bancroft, History of California II (1885), 296-98 and 630-32, for the founding, the garrison and the artillery of Ross.

For the San Francisco comparison: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. i.1110-1113 / Savage pp. 261-263 / scan n260-n262, Doc 332. Manuel Gómez's report of 20 March 1820: eight cannon, two of them unserviceable, and not a single veteran artilleryman.

features.notes: Both the Ross figure (a Spanish estimate) and the SF figure (a Spanish self-inventory) are Spanish-sourced, so the comparison is internally consistent. The defensible claim is order-of-magnitude parity, not a precise gun-for-gun ratio.

features.name: Presidio of San Francisco
features.summary: 1776. Northernmost military post. $1,400 total investment by 1793. Garrison: ~35 men.

features.name: Fort San Joaquín (Castillo de SF)
features.summary: 1794. Battery guarding the Golden Gate narrows. 1 cannon (burst 1792), 8 by 1793, 6 functional by 1820. Unmanned by 1800.

features.name: Mission San Rafael
features.summary: 1817. Anti-Russian buffer. 83 days after Hagemeister treaty. Founded without a boat.

features.name: Bodega y Quadra discovers and charts the port
features.summary: The schooner Sonora under Bodega y Quadra and pilot Francisco Mourelle charts the port on the return leg of the 1775 voyage. Their manuscript plano, with keyed points and soundings, is the founding document of the Spanish claim. The chart is in this site's gallery.
features.result: The port charted and claimed

sources.citation: Plano del Puerto del Capitan Bodega (LOC, gallery item loc-bq05); resurveyed 1793 (Cartas esfericas sheet 8)
Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms: El Puerto de la Bodega and Bodega Bay' (1964) · identifies the 1775 anchorage as Tomales Bay
Wagner, Sir Francis Drake's Voyage Around the World (1926), 158–59 · reads the chart as Bodega Harbor

features.notes: Which water the Sonora actually entered is disputed: Edwards (1964) and Beals identify Tomales Bay, Wagner (1926) Bodega Harbor; see the hollow companion point for the Tomales reading.

features.name: The 1793 occupation attempt fails
features.summary: The year Spain finally moved to occupy Bodega: Matute's establishment attempt, mounted amid the Nootka crisis, was abandoned. The port Spain had claimed in 1775 stayed empty, and the re-survey of the same year became its monument. The full argument is the subject of the companion article.
features.result: Spain never occupied the port it discovered

sources.citation: C-A 55 (Matute dossier); the 1793 re-survey, Cartas esfericas sheet 8 (gallery)

features.notes: Deliberately summary-level here; the article carries the argument and the full citations.

features.name: The 1811 Aleut otter fleet in San Francisco Bay
features.summary: Russian-American Company hunting reaches inside the bay itself. On 30 May 1811 Argüello reported Aleut baidarkas working the port, up to fifty together, and some 130 counted between Punta Bonita and Punta San Antonio; six neophytes sent across to fish sea lions for their padres were held for some hours as suspected spies before being released. Spain's inner waters were a Russian hunting ground a year before Ross was founded.

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 12) Doc 381 · Argüello, San Francisco, 30 May 1811: the otter-fishing canoes still working inside the port, up to 50 seen together, and ~130 counted between Puntas de Boneta and San Antonio.
Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 12) Doc 334 · the same hunt a year earlier: ~20 canoes heading into the San José esteros, and gentiles reporting a large ship at Bodega.

features.name: Vallejo's reconnaissance of Ross (informe reservado)
features.summary: M. G. Vallejo's confidential report on Ross: about 300 people, a wooden stockade, cannon in the towers, and Russian-American Company intelligence gathered through Wrangel's circle. The fullest Mexican-era picture of the colony, twenty years in.

sources.citation: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53), Doc 45 (n97–n111)

features.name: Ross sold to Sutter; the Russians withdraw
features.summary: The Russian-American Company sells the Ross establishment to John Sutter and withdraws from California, ending the colony the Spanish had watched for thirty years without ever dislodging.
features.result: The Russian era ends by sale, not by force

sources.citation: Duflot de Mofras (1844) records the post-sale coast; cf. the borderlands map's abandonment-resolved pin

features.name: Port Rumiantsev (Bodega Bay)
features.summary: ~1807. RAC fur-collecting base. First representative: Tarakanov. Permanent.
features.notes: Anchorage in Bodega Harbor; the precise landing/port site is approximate.

features.name: Kostromitinov Ranch
features.summary: 1833. Russian River near Willow Creek. ~100 acres wheat by 1841.
features.notes: Exact ranch site debated (Osborn); descriptions place it on the south side of the Russian River near its mouth.

features.name: Khlebnikov Ranch
features.summary: 1833. Upper Salmon Creek valley, ~5 mi E of Bodega. Largest ranch; bakery, forge, tobacco shed.

features.name: Chernykh Ranch
features.summary: ~1833. Near Graton (Purrington Creek). First vineyard in Sonoma County.

features.name: Matute on the Sutil · the Occupation Refused
features.summary: Naval lieutenant Juan Bautista Matute arrives on the Sutil to plant the Bodega settlement, finds no English, and refuses to carry out the occupation: the harbor too shallow for the mission, no timber, no building material. He takes his artisans and troops back to San Blas in October; the quiet end of Spain's last northward move. If Edwards is right about the 1775 name, Matute was also surveying a different water than the one Bodega had praised.
features.result: Occupation abandoned

sources.citation: Matute's resultas of the Bodega commission (AGN, Historia 71)
Matute's 1793 plan of Bodega (AHN, Estado, MPD. 33)
Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms' (1964) · the wrong-harbor argument

features.name: The 1775 Anchorage · the Tomales Reading
features.summary: Edwards's reconstruction: the water the Sonora entered on October 3, 1775; the original 'Puerto de la Bodega'; was Tomales Bay. Beals's edition of Bodega's journal reaches the same identification. Everything on the modern map called Bodega carries a migrated name.
features.result: Identification debated

sources.citation: Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms' (1964)
Beals (ed.), For Honor and Country: the diary of Bodega y Quadra (Hakluyt, 2007), editorial note

features.notes: Drawn hollow: a scholarly reconstruction, not a documented position.

features.name: San Rafael Attacked · the Piña Expedition
features.summary: Mission San Rafael, its founding padre Amorós just dead and its population collapsing, is attacked by gentiles; an expedition goes out under Lázaro Piña. Word of the rising carries through fugitive mission Indians to the Ross-area rancherías; the likely referent of the Russians' report of a 'spring 1832 San Rafael revolt'.
features.result: The North Bay crisis opens

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California III, 716 (citing Vallejo, Documentos, MS, i.307)
Bolkhovitinov & Istomin, Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki III, ch. 6 (the Russian report)

features.name: Kashaya Resistance at Ross
features.summary: With the otter gone and Ross living off its grain, manager Kostromitinov's parties seize Kashaya laborers by force; Wrangell records up to 150 gathered, families 'driven to the settlement like cattle to work'. Kashaya and Miwok answer with five years of attacks on company property, culminating in an 1838 raid that kills about a hundred Ross cattle. Indian resistance becomes one cause of the colony's unprofitability and sale.
features.result: Resistance presses on the colony's economics

sources.citation: Wrangell and Kostromitonov, ethnographic reports (Stross trans., 1974)
Bolkhovitinov & Istomin, Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki III, ch. 6

features.name: RAC Possession Plate No. 14 · Malaya Bodega
features.summary: Kuskov's expedition buries numbered metal claiming plate No. 14 at 'Malaya Bodega,' the inner harbor; one of a chain of iron plates with brass crosses by which the company staked New Albion years before Ross was built (No. 1 at Trinidad, 1808).
features.result: The coast staked in metal

sources.citation: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12)
Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)

features.name: RAC Possession Plate No. 20 · Drake's Estero
features.summary: A second numbered claiming plate buried at the mouth of Drake's Estero; the company quietly marking the shore of New Albion down to 38°.

sources.citation: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12)
Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)

features.name: The Buried Eagle · a Plate in San Pablo Bay
features.summary: The company later reported placing 'plate No. 1000 and one coat of arms'; a double-headed eagle; at 'Malaya Bodega, in the northern arm of San Francisco, where the fort and mission of the Spaniards were built': a possession marker buried inside the Spanish bay itself, in the waters of San Pablo Bay. Its spot has never been found.
features.result: A claim buried inside Spanish waters

sources.citation: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12)
Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)

features.notes: Position conjectural; drawn hollow; the RAC report's geography is ambiguous.

routes.label: Moraga October 1810; Bodega Reconnaissance
routes.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 12) Doc 335 — Moraga's own diary of the Bodega expedition, 23 Sep–2 Oct 1810 (Savage pp. 276–279, the leaves Langelier & Rosen cite at fn. 52). Indians at the estero de San Juan Francisco reported a frigate at Bodega and two Unalaska men who had come that morning to look at it.

stops.name: Presidio of San Francisco
stops.summary: October 3, 1810. Governor orders Moraga to investigate Russian fur-hunting at Bodega Bay. 10-day reconnaissance.

sources.citation: Langelier & Rosen, fn. 52: 'Gabriel Moraga's Diary of his Expedition to the Port of Bodega, Oct. 3, 1810, Prov. St. Pap., XII, 276–79.' Diary survives in the Archives of California.

stops.name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
stops.summary: Crossed the bay from the Presidio to the Marin shore. Method uncertain — possibly native balsas or a borrowed vessel.

sources.citation: SF Presidio had limited boat access. See boat-problem article.

stops.name: San Rafael Area
stops.summary: Passed through future site of Mission San Rafael. Bancroft: 'The site was probably selected on the advice of Moraga, who had several times passed it on his way to and from Bodega.'

sources.citation: Bancroft, II, p. 330.

stops.name: Novato / Olompali Area
stops.summary: Route north through Marin. Approximate — following the natural corridor through the Novato gap toward Petaluma Creek and the coast.

sources.citation: Exact route not specified in diary abstract.

stops.name: Petaluma Creek / Estuary
stops.summary: Likely crossed or followed Petaluma Creek toward the coast. Natural route from interior Marin to Bodega Bay.

sources.citation: Route reconstruction based on geography.

stops.name: Bodega Bay
stops.summary: Arrived at Bodega Bay. Found an American ship and Alaskan Indians (Aleut hunters working for the Russian-American Company). 10-day reconnaissance of the area. Wrote a diary of the expedition.

sources.citation: Langelier & Rosen: 'finds an American ship and Alaskan Indians.' Diary: Prov. St. Pap., XII, 276–79.

stops.name: Return to Presidio
stops.summary: Returns after 10 days. Report confirms Russian presence and fur-hunting operations at Bodega.

routes.label: Moraga 1812; First Visit to Ross
routes.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 12) Doc 407 — Argüello reports Moraga's second reconnaissance, returned 1 September 1812. Cf. Langelier & Rosen, ch. 3.

stops.name: Presidio of San Francisco
stops.summary: July 1812. Argüello sends Moraga with 4 men to investigate construction of a small Russian fort on the Sonoma coast. Fort Ross had been dedicated Sept. 10, 1812 — but Kuskov had been building since spring.

sources.citation: Langelier & Rosen, Ch. 3.

stops.name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
stops.summary: Crossed the bay to the Marin shore.

stops.name: San Rafael Area
stops.summary: Through future Mission San Rafael site. Moraga's repeated passage through here informed his later recommendation of the site.

stops.name: Petaluma Creek Area
stops.summary: North through Marin toward the coast. Approximate route.

stops.name: Bodega Bay
stops.summary: Passed through or near Bodega Bay en route to Fort Ross.

stops.name: Fort Ross
stops.summary: Moraga identifies the Russian settlement: a brigantine-anchored base with a 150-yard-square stockade and cannon. Notes the Russians' friendly manner. Fort Ross had been dedicated by Kuskov with 95 Russians and ~80 Aleut hunters.

sources.citation: Langelier & Rosen: '150-yard-square stockade and cannon; notes the Russians' friendly manner.'

stops.name: Return to Presidio
stops.summary: Returns to SF. Report filed with Argüello.

routes.label: Moraga 1813; Second Ross Mission
routes.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 12) Doc 439 — Moraga's reconnaissance and defence assessment of Ross: artillery could not reach it without a better road; about forty *personas de razón* and many Kodiaks. Cf. Langelier & Rosen, ch. 3.

stops.name: Presidio of San Francisco
stops.summary: January 1813. Moraga drives 20 cattle and 3 horses to Fort Ross — practical diplomacy. Returns again in 1814 with Cadet Gervasio Argüello.

sources.citation: Langelier & Rosen, Ch. 3.

stops.name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
stops.summary: Crossed bay to Marin shore with livestock.

stops.name: San Rafael Area
stops.summary: Through future mission site, driving cattle north.

stops.name: Bodega Bay Area
stops.summary: Through Bodega country toward Fort Ross.

stops.name: Fort Ross
stops.summary: Jan. 1813: Delivered 20 cattle, 3 horses as goodwill gesture. 1814 return: accompanied by Cadet Gervasio Argüello. Wrote a report describing 40 gente de razón and many Kodiak Indians, cannon, glass windows in the commandant's house. Also carried official demands for Russian withdrawal.

sources.citation: Langelier & Rosen: '40 gente de razón and many Kodiak Indians, cannon guarding the place, and glass windows in the commandant's house.'

stops.name: Return to Presidio
stops.summary: Returns to SF Presidio.
